extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and legal scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Rules governing the rights, duties, and remedies of joint owners, grantees, licensors, executors, and administrators in relation to patented inventions under U.S. law. Includes how ownership vests on death, what powers individual co-owners have to practice, assign, or license, and how profits, liability, and suits are apportioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenancy in common of joint patentees
rubrics_metrics.description: Joint-owners of a patented invention are tenants in common; each has the right to make, use, and sell the invention within his share and may practise the invention without accountability to the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule preserves the nature of the monopoly and permits each owner wide latitude in enjoyment of the invention. Each joint-owner may himself practise the invention and may convey his entire interest to another individual; but the ownership is undivided and subordinate rights are individually possessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on alienation by a joint-owner (multiplying practitioners)
rubrics_metrics.description: A joint-owner may not grant assignments or licenses that multiply the number of persons who can lawfully practise the invention in a way that sensibly diminishes the value of the patent to other owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While a joint-owner may convey his interest to another single owner, he is forbidden (without consent of co-owners) to assign his interest to several assignees or grant widespread licenses because that would increase the burden on the common property and possibly destroy its value. Courts treat this as a restriction to conserve the monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of a license by one co-owner
rubrics_metrics.description: A license granted by one co-owner is valid against third parties and, in many cases, good as against the other co-owners; the other co-owners' remedy is generally an action for account against the licensor rather than an injunction against the licensee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (e.g., De Witt v. Elmira Nobles; Curran v. Burdsall) hold that estoppel against the assignor/licensor operates as a license to the third party, and the other patentees must look to the assignor for an account. Some decisions disfavor issuing injunctions against such licensees in suits by co-owners.

rubrics_metrics.name: No general duty to account for mere use (subject to exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: One co-owner generally cannot be compelled to account to another merely for using the patented invention or for profits from such mere use; but if he obtains more than his share (e.g., from licenses or sales), he may under certain circumstances be held accountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise cautions that while there is no absolute rule forcing accounting for every use, equitable principles (and specific circumstances or contracts between co-owners) can give rise to liability. Courts have reached differing conclusions depending on facts and prior agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint-owner liability for practicing infringing inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A joint-owner who uses or employs an infringing art or instrument (i.e., acts outside the precise acts involved in the practice of the patented invention) is not shielded by his ownership and is liable as a stranger for infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ownership of the patent and the monopoly does not entitle a co-owner to perform acts which would be infringement if done by a stranger. Licensees who practice beyond the scope of their license are likewise liable. Recovery for such infringement is apportioned among co-owners according to their interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal relations modifiable by contract
rubrics_metrics.description: The general rules between joint-owners govern in the absence of contract, but co-owners are free to regulate their reciprocal rights by agreement (e.g., to account, to restrict alienation, to appoint agents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreements can increase, diminish, or change the character of co-owners' rights and may create continuing duties (e.g., to account) that can bind successors or be enforced in equity; such agreements may have consequences under statute of frauds principles if not executed within a year, but executed transfers can validate ongoing agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suits and remedies involving joint-owners and third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement by a stranger violates the right of all joint-owners; suits against strangers should be brought in the names of all joint-owners and damages are distributed among them according to their respective undivided interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a stranger infringes, all joint-owners must join to redress the wrong; when a co-owner is the infringer, other joint-owners should ordinarily be plaintiffs and recovery will be apportioned by interest. Estoppel may make assignees/licensees effective against co-owners, leaving co-owners to seek account from the licensor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint grantees and territorial limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Joint grantees who hold territorially limited rights occupy toward each other the same relations as joint-owners of the entire interest; within their local boundaries they possess complete property and monopoly and may practise, dispose of, or license the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their rights may be modified by agreement; owners of different territorial interests may combine privileges or contract to change their rights as otherwise defined by law. Within a grantee's territory the monopoly is indivisible among those grantees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vesting of decedent's patent interest in executor/administrator
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon death, the decedent's interest in a patented invention vests immediately in his executor or administrator by virtue of federal statutes; the executor/administrator holds the title under patent laws of the United States rather than local state probate law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The executor/administrator must prosecute pending applications, may file new applications where inventor died pending application, and may sue for infringement; his authority and the nature of his ownership are governed by acts of Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the patent interest in hands of executor/administrator
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent in the hands of an executor or administrator is not personalty of the decedent's estate nor assets liable to creditors; it is a franchise held in a special capacity under the Patent Laws, not a ordinary estate asset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though often described as a trustee, the administrator is a statutory instrument charged to manage the franchise for the benefit of heirs or devisees, and his dealings with the patent are governed by federal patent law rather than local property rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executor/administrator relations to heirs and devisees
rubrics_metrics.description: As between the executor/administrator and the heirs/devisees, the beneficial interest vests in the heirs/devisees even though the executor manages and controls the patent; to third parties and the Patent Office the executor's title appears identical with the decedent's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In procuring patents, reissues, extensions, prosecuting infringement suits, making contracts and licenses, the executor acts as if independent owner but is accountable in equity to those holding the beneficial interest (heirs or devisees).

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel and effect of assignments on co-owners' remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Where one joint-patentee assigns or estops himself by conduct, that assignment may operate as a license to a third party and preclude other patentees from enjoining the third party; the other patentees' remedy may be limited to accounting against the assignor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court decisions recognize that an assignee or licensee under one co-owner may be protected from suit by the other co-owners (who must instead seek redress from the assignor), and that this can materially affect enforcement of the monopoly among co-owners and third parties.
